da-2026-2-da-4.approach: Apply Bayes' theorem with the three given rates: the positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positives. Natural frequencies (out of 10 000 people) make the arithmetic transparent.
da-2026-2-da-4.given:
| Quantity | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Prevalence | $P(D)$ | $0.01$ |
| Sensitivity | $P(+\mid D)$ | $0.95$ |
| Specificity | $P(-\mid \bar D)$ | $0.90$ |
| False-positive rate | $P(+\mid \bar D) = 1-0.90$ | $0.10$ |

steps.title: Turn the rates into probabilities
steps.body: Specificity is the probability of a **negative** result for a healthy person, so a healthy person tests positive with probability $P(+\mid\bar D) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10$. Also $P(\bar D) = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99$.

steps.title: Total probability of a positive test
Bayes' theorem
steps.body:
$$P(D\mid +) = \frac{P(+\mid D)P(D)}{P(+)} = \frac{0.0095}{0.1085} = 0.08756\ldots \approx 0.0876$$
So only about **8.8 %** of people who test positive actually have the disease.

steps.title: Same result with natural frequencies
steps.body: Out of $10\,000$ people: $100$ are ill, of whom $0.95 \times 100 = 95$ test positive; $9\,900$ are healthy, of whom $0.10 \times 9\,900 = 990$ test positive. Positives $= 95 + 990 = 1085$, so $P(D\mid +) = \frac{95}{1085} \approx 0.0876$.

optionAnalysis.reason: This is the sensitivity $P(+\mid D)$ — confusing $P(+\mid D)$ with $P(D\mid +)$ (the inverse-probability fallacy).
No calculation gives 0.5; it treats a positive result as a coin flip and ignores both the base rate and the test rates.
This is the prior (prevalence) $P(D)$ — ignoring the evidence of the positive test altogether.

da-2026-2-da-4.shortcut: Ratio form: $\frac{0.95 \times 1}{0.95 \times 1 + 0.10 \times 99} = \frac{0.95}{10.85} \approx 0.088$ — scale both terms by 100 and divide.
pitfalls: Using the specificity 0.90 as the false-positive rate; the false-positive rate is $1 - 0.90 = 0.10$.
Answering the sensitivity (0.95): $P(+\mid D) \ne P(D\mid +)$.
Ignoring the 1 % base rate — with a rare disease, false positives from the large healthy group dominate.
da-2026-2-da-4.verification: Natural-frequency count (95 true positives vs 990 false positives) gives $95/1085 = 0.08756$, matching the formula. Sanity check: the posterior (8.8 %) rose from the prior (1 %), as a positive result should make the disease more likely.

da-2026-2-da-5.approach: Worst case for separate chaining is the adversarial input where every key hashes to the same slot: the table degenerates into one linked list of length $n$, and an (unsuccessful) search scans all of it.

steps.title: How a search works with chaining
steps.body: Search for key $k$: compute $h(k)$ in $O(1)$, then walk the linked list (chain) stored in slot $h(k)$, comparing $k$ with each element. Cost $= O(1) + O(\text{length of that chain})$.

steps.title: Worst case: all keys collide
steps.body: Nothing stops all $n$ keys from hashing to the same slot (e.g. a poor hash function or adversarial keys). Then one chain holds all $n$ elements, and the other $m-1$ slots are empty.

scene.caption: Searching for an absent key compares it with all $n$ nodes.

steps.title: Cost of the search
steps.body: Searching for a key that is absent (or at the tail) compares it with all $n$ elements of that chain: $\Theta(1) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n)$. The table size $m$ does not matter here.

steps.title: Contrast with the average case
steps.body: Under simple uniform hashing the expected chain length is the load factor $\alpha = n/m$, giving $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ on average — which is $\Theta(1)$ only when $n = O(m)$. The question asks for the **worst** case: $\Theta(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: all $n$ keys can fall in one chain, so a search may compare against all $n$ of them.
This is the *average* case with a constant load factor ($\Theta(1+\alpha)$, $\alpha = O(1)$), not the worst case.
Logarithmic time would need a balanced search tree in each bucket; plain chaining uses linked lists.
The chain length depends on $n$, not on the table size $m$; even scanning every slot is not the cost of one chained search.

da-2026-2-da-5.shortcut: Worst case of any hashing scheme = "everything collides" → linear in the number of stored keys.
pitfalls: Quoting the textbook $O(1)$ — that is the expected time under uniform hashing.
Writing $\Theta(n/m)$: that is the average chain length, not the worst one.
da-2026-2-da-5.verification: CLRS §11.2: "The worst-case behavior of hashing with chaining is terrible: all $n$ keys hash to the same slot, creating a list of length $n$. The worst-case time for searching is thus $\Theta(n)$" (paraphrased).

animation.caption: All $n$ keys hash to the same slot; the other $m-1$ slots are empty.

da-2026-2-da-6.approach: With a closed list, A* never re-expands a node, so the first time a node is expanded its $g$ must already be optimal. Consistency ($h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')$) guarantees exactly that; admissibility alone does not, as a 5-node counterexample shows.
concepts: Graph search with a closed list

steps.title: The two properties
steps.body:
- **Admissible:** $h(n) \le h^*(n)$ (never overestimates the true cost to the goal).
- **Consistent:** $h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')$ for every edge $n \to n'$, and $h(\text{goal}) = 0$. Consistent ⇒ admissible, not conversely.

steps.title: Why consistency suffices
steps.body: If $h$ is consistent, then along any path $f(n') = g(n) + c(n,n') + h(n') \ge g(n) + h(n) = f(n)$: $f$ never decreases. Hence A* expands nodes in non-decreasing $f$ order, and when a node is first expanded (and moved to the closed list) it has been reached by an optimal path. Never reopening it is therefore safe, and the goal is returned with optimal cost.

steps.title: Admissible-only counterexample: setup
steps.body: In the graph, $h$ is admissible ($h(A)=4 \le 4$, $h(B)=1 \le 5$, $h(C)=1 \le 3$) but **inconsistent** on edge $A \to C$: $h(A) = 4 > c(A,C) + h(C) = 1 + 1 = 2$. The optimal path is $S\!-\!A\!-\!C\!-\!G$ with cost $1+1+3 = 5$.

steps.title: Run A*: C is closed via the worse path
steps.body: Expand $S$: $f(A) = 1 + 4 = 5$, $f(B) = 1 + 1 = 2$. Expand $B$ (smallest $f$): $C$ gets $g = 1 + 2 = 3$, $f = 3 + 1 = 4$. Expand $C$ ($f = 4 < 5$) and **close** it with $g(C) = 3$; $G$ gets $g = 3 + 3 = 6$, $f = 6$.

steps.title: Run A*: the better path is discarded
steps.body: Expand $A$ ($f = 5$): it reaches $C$ with $g = 1 + 1 = 2 < 3$, but $C$ is already closed, so the improvement is ignored. Next $G$ ($f = 6$) is selected and returned with cost **6 ≠ 5**. Admissibility alone fails; consistency is the property required.

scene.caption: Returned cost 6 via S–B–C–G; optimal is 5 via S–A–C–G.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: a consistent heuristic makes $f$ non-decreasing along paths, so every node is closed with its optimal $g$ and A* graph search is optimal.
Admissibility guarantees optimality for **tree** search (or graph search that reopens closed nodes), but not for graph search with a closed list — see the counterexample.
Convexity is a property of functions in continuous optimisation; it has no role in A*'s optimality conditions.
Linear separability concerns classification datasets (perceptron/SVM), not search heuristics.

da-2026-2-da-6.shortcut: Tree search → admissible is enough; graph search with a closed list (no reopening) → need consistent.
pitfalls: Answering "admissible" from memory of tree-search A*; the phrase "closed lists" is the clue.
Forgetting that consistency implies admissibility (so "consistency" is the stronger, sufficient condition).
da-2026-2-da-6.verification: Russell & Norvig (AIMA, §3.5): "the tree-search version of A* is optimal if $h(n)$ is admissible, while the graph-search version is optimal if $h(n)$ is consistent" — matches the counterexample, where A* with a closed list returns 6 instead of 5.

animation.title: Admissible but inconsistent h breaks A* with a closed list
animation.caption: Badges show $h$. True costs to G: $h^*(A)=4$, $h^*(B)=5$, $h^*(C)=3$ — so $h$ is admissible.

da-2026-2-da-7.approach: Classify the dimensional-modelling schemas by two features: how many fact tables there are, and whether dimension tables are normalised into sub-dimension hierarchies. One fact table + flat (denormalised) dimensions is the star schema.

steps.title: Star schema
steps.body: One central **fact table** (measures + foreign keys) joined directly to each **dimension table**. Each dimension is a single, **denormalised** table (e.g. Product holds product, category and brand columns together), so there are no dimension-to-dimension links — the diagram looks like a star.

steps.title: Snowflake schema
steps.body: Same central fact table, but dimensions are **normalised** into hierarchies (Product → Category → Department), giving dimension-to-dimension joins — the "snowflake" branches.

steps.title: Galaxy / constellation
steps.body: **Several fact tables** share common (conformed) dimensions. "Galaxy schema" and "fact constellation" are two names for the same design; neither is defined by a single centralised fact table.

steps.title: Match the description
steps.body:
| Schema | Fact tables | Dimensions | Dim-to-dim links |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Star** | 1 | denormalised | none |
| Snowflake | 1 | normalised | yes |
| Galaxy / constellation | many | shared | (either) |

The description — one central fact table, fully denormalised dimensions, zero hierarchies — is the **star schema**.

optionAnalysis.reason: A galaxy schema has **multiple** fact tables sharing dimensions, not one centralised fact table.
Constellation (fact constellation) is the same as galaxy: multiple fact tables.
Correct: single fact table, each dimension a flat denormalised table joined directly to it.
Snowflake normalises dimensions into hierarchies, creating exactly the dimension-to-dimension links the question excludes.

da-2026-2-da-7.shortcut: "Denormalised dimensions" ⇒ star; "normalised dimensions" ⇒ snowflake; "many fact tables" ⇒ galaxy/constellation.
pitfalls: Treating galaxy and constellation as different schemas — they are synonyms, which also rules both out together.
da-2026-2-da-7.verification: Kimball's dimensional-modelling definitions: star = denormalised dimensions around one fact table; snowflaking = normalising a dimension into sub-tables.

da-2026-2-da-8.approach: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives $(f_x, f_y)$. Differentiate once in each variable, holding the other constant, then substitute $(1,-1)$.

steps.title: Partial derivative in $x$
steps.body: Treat $y$ as a constant: $f_x = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3x^2y - 4y^3 + 2x) = 6xy - 0 + 2 = 6xy + 2$.

steps.title: Partial derivative in $y$
steps.body: Treat $x$ as a constant: $f_y = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(3x^2y - 4y^3 + 2x) = 3x^2 - 12y^2 + 0 = 3x^2 - 12y^2$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Drops the $6xy$ term from $f_x$ (giving 2) and the $3x^2$ term from $f_y$ (giving $-12$) — differentiating only some terms.
Right $f_x$, but evaluates $-12y^2$ as $+12$ at $y=-1$ (sign slip on the square), giving $3 + 12 = 15$.
Right $f_y$, but takes $6xy = +6$ (ignoring $y = -1$), giving $6 + 2 = 8$ for $f_x$.

da-2026-2-da-8.shortcut: Compute only $f_x(1,-1) = 6(1)(-1)+2 = -4$: it already eliminates (B) and (D); then $f_y = 3 - 12 = -9$ picks (A) over (C).
pitfalls: Forgetting the constant term $2$ in $f_x$ (from $2x$).

da-2026-2-da-9.approach: Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps — assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points — and each step can only decrease the same quantity: the within-cluster sum of squared distances.

steps.title: The objective
steps.body:
$$J = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \sum_{x_i \in C_j} \lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2$$
the **within-cluster sum of squares** (WCSS, also called inertia or distortion).

steps.title: Assignment step lowers $J$
steps.body: With centroids fixed, assigning each $x_i$ to its nearest $\mu_j$ minimises its own term $\lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2$, so $J$ cannot increase.

steps.title: Update step lowers $J$
steps.body: With assignments fixed, $\sum_{x_i \in C_j}\lVert x_i - \mu \rVert^2$ is minimised at $\mu = \frac{1}{\lvert C_j\rvert}\sum_{x_i \in C_j} x_i$ (set the gradient $-2\sum (x_i - \mu) = 0$), i.e. the cluster mean. So $J$ again cannot increase.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Lloyd's algorithm is coordinate descent on WCSS; it converges (to a local minimum) because WCSS decreases monotonically and there are finitely many partitions.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: both the assignment and the mean-update step minimise $\sum_j \sum_{x_i \in C_j}\lVert x_i - \mu_j\rVert^2$.
Between-cluster separation is something one would *maximise*; k-means does not optimise a separation ratio directly (that resembles the Calinski–Harabasz index).
The silhouette coefficient is a post-hoc evaluation metric (to be maximised), not the training objective.
KL divergence compares probability distributions (e.g. t-SNE, variational methods); it is not k-means' objective.

da-2026-2-da-9.shortcut: K-means = minimise squared distance to the cluster mean = WCSS ("inertia" in scikit-learn).
pitfalls: Confusing evaluation metrics (silhouette) with the objective the algorithm optimises.
da-2026-2-da-9.verification: Because total sum of squares = WCSS + between-cluster SS is constant for fixed data, minimising WCSS also maximises between-cluster SS — but the quantity Lloyd's steps directly minimise is WCSS.

da-2026-2-da-10.approach: Use the convolution output-size formula $O = \frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1$ on the spatial dimensions; the filter depth (3) matches the input depth and only produces one output channel.
da-2026-2-da-10.given:
| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $W$ | input width/height | 32 |
| $F$ | filter size | 5 |
| $P$ | padding | 0 |
| $S$ | stride | 1 |

steps.title: Output-size formula
steps.body: Each spatial dimension of the output is $O = \left\lfloor \frac{W - F + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body:
$$O = \frac{32 - 5 + 2(0)}{1} + 1 = 27 + 1 = 28$$
Same for height, so the feature map is $28 \times 28$.

steps.title: What the depth does
steps.body: The filter is $5 \times 5 \times 3$: its depth equals the input depth, so it slides only in 2-D and produces **one** $28 \times 28$ channel (with $k$ filters, the output is $28 \times 28 \times k$).

optionAnalysis.reason: Would need $F = 3$ ($32 - 3 + 1 = 30$) — e.g. mistakenly using the depth 3 as the filter size.
Forgets the $+1$: $32 - 5 = 27$.
This is the "same" padding result ($P = 2$); the question says no padding.

da-2026-2-da-10.shortcut: Stride 1, no padding: output side $= W - F + 1 = 32 - 5 + 1 = 28$.
pitfalls: Dropping the $+1$ (count of valid positions is $W - F + 1$, not $W - F$).
Letting the channel depth change the spatial size.
da-2026-2-da-10.verification: Count positions: the filter's left edge can sit at columns $0, 1, \dots, 27$ (it needs columns up to $27 + 4 = 31$, the last column) — that is 28 positions.

da-2026-2-da-11.approach: Recall the definition: a real square matrix is orthogonal when its columns (and rows) are orthonormal, which is exactly $Q^TQ = I$; for square matrices this forces $Q^{-1} = Q^T$ and hence also $QQ^T = I$.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Entry $(i,j)$ of $Q^TQ$ is $q_i \cdot q_j$ (dot product of columns $i$ and $j$). Columns are orthonormal ⇔ $q_i \cdot q_j = \delta_{ij}$ ⇔ $Q^TQ = I$.

steps.title: Square ⇒ both products are $I$
steps.body: For a square matrix, $Q^TQ = I$ means $Q^T$ is a left inverse, hence the inverse: $Q^{-1} = Q^T$, so also $QQ^T = I$. Thus "$Q^TQ = QQ^T = I$" is an exact characterisation.

steps.title: Check the distractors with examples
steps.body:
- Symmetric but not orthogonal: $\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ ($Q^TQ = 4I$).
- Idempotent: $Q^2 = Q$ holds for projections like $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$, which is singular, not orthogonal.
- $\det Q = 0$ is impossible: $\det(Q^TQ) = (\det Q)^2 = 1$, so $\det Q = \pm 1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $Q = Q^T$ defines a **symmetric** matrix; e.g. $2I$ is symmetric but not orthogonal, and a rotation by 90° is orthogonal but not symmetric.
$Q^2 = Q$ defines an **idempotent** (projection) matrix; non-identity projections are singular, so not orthogonal.
Correct: orthonormal columns and rows, i.e. $Q^{-1} = Q^T$.
Orthogonal matrices have $\det Q = \pm 1$, never 0 — they are always invertible.

pitfalls: Mixing up "orthogonal" with "symmetric" because both involve the transpose.

steps.title: Variance of $X$
steps.body: For $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $E[X] = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$.

steps.title: Linear transformation
steps.body: $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2 \operatorname{Var}(X)$: adding a constant shifts every value equally and leaves deviations from the mean unchanged; scaling by $a$ scales deviations by $a$ and squared deviations by $a^2$.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: $$\operatorname{Var}(3X + 5) = 3^2 \times 4 = 9 \times 4 = 36$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: $3^2 \times 4 = 36$.
$3 \times 4 + 5 = 17$ — this is $E[Y]$, the mean, not the variance.
$3 \times 4 = 12$ — scales by $a$ instead of $a^2$.
$9 \times 4 + 5 = 41$ — wrongly adds the constant 5 to the variance.

da-2026-2-da-12.shortcut: Constants added vanish; constants multiplied come out squared: $9\lambda = 36$.
pitfalls: Adding the shift $b$ to the variance.
Using $a$ instead of $a^2$.

da-2026-2-da-13.approach: Match the argument form $P,\ P \to Q \vdash Q$ against the standard rules of inference; it is the defining pattern of modus ponens ("affirming the antecedent").

steps.title: The rules side by side
steps.body:
| Rule | Premises | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| **Modus ponens** | $P,\ P \to Q$ | $Q$ |
| Modus tollens | $\neg Q,\ P \to Q$ | $\neg P$ |
| Resolution | $P \lor Q,\ \neg P \lor R$ | $Q \lor R$ |
| Hypothetical syllogism | $P \to Q,\ Q \to R$ | $P \to R$ |

steps.title: Match the given argument
steps.body: The given premises are $P$ and $P \to Q$ and the conclusion is $Q$ — exactly the modus ponens pattern ("affirming the antecedent").

steps.title: Why it is valid
steps.body:
| $P$ | $Q$ | $P \to Q$ | premises both true? |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | **yes** → $Q$ = T |
| T | F | F | no |
| F | T | T | no |
| F | F | T | no |

In the only row where both premises hold, $Q$ is true, so $(P \land (P \to Q)) \to Q$ is a tautology.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: from $P$ and $P \to Q$, infer $Q$.
Modus tollens goes the other way: from $\neg Q$ and $P \to Q$ infer $\neg P$.
Resolution works on clauses $P \lor Q,\ \neg P \lor R \vdash Q \lor R$; it can *simulate* modus ponens (write $P \to Q$ as $\neg P \lor Q$), but the named rule for this form is modus ponens.
Hypothetical syllogism chains implications: $P \to Q,\ Q \to R \vdash P \to R$; it does not take a bare fact $P$.

da-2026-2-da-13.shortcut: Ponens "puts" (affirms) the antecedent; tollens "takes away" (denies) the consequent.
pitfalls: Swapping ponens and tollens.
da-2026-2-da-13.verification: Truth table of $(P \land (P\to Q)) \to Q$: true in all four rows, so the inference is valid.

da-2026-2-da-14.approach: A moving average needs, for each row, an aggregate over a sliding set of neighbouring rows while keeping every row in the output — that is a window function, written with an `OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY … [ROWS …])` clause.

steps.title: What a moving average needs
steps.body: For each row (e.g. each day of each store) compute `AVG(sales)` over that row and the previous few rows *of the same store, in date order*. The result must be one value **per row**, not one per group.

steps.title: The window clause does exactly that
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT store, day, sales,
       AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY store
                        ORDER BY day
                        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7
FROM daily_sales;
```
`PARTITION BY` splits rows into independent windows (per store), `ORDER BY` fixes the order inside each, and the frame (`ROWS BETWEEN …`) makes the window slide.

steps.title: Why the others do not
steps.body: `GROUP BY ROLLUP` collapses rows into groups plus hierarchical subtotals; `HAVING` filters groups; `PIVOT` turns row values into columns. None computes a per-row sliding aggregate.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: the window clause partitions, orders, and (with a frame) slides the aggregate row by row — the standard way to compute moving averages.
`ROLLUP` produces subtotals and a grand total along a hierarchy; it aggregates rows away rather than computing a rolling window.
`HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` only filters groups after `GROUP BY`.
`PIVOT` reshapes rows into columns (cross-tab); it does not define windows.

da-2026-2-da-14.shortcut: "Rolling"/"moving"/"running" anything in SQL ⇒ window function with `OVER (…)`.
pitfalls: Confusing "roll-up" (OLAP drill-up/subtotals) with "rolling" (sliding-window) aggregates.
da-2026-2-da-14.verification: SQL:2003 window functions (supported by PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Hive/Spark SQL) are the documented mechanism for moving averages; `ROLLUP` is part of grouping-sets syntax.

da-2026-2-da-15.approach: Use the second-order Taylor expansion at a critical point: the gradient term vanishes, so the sign of the quadratic form $d^T \nabla^2 f(x^*) d$ decides the nature of the point. Positive for every $d \ne 0$ (positive definite) ⇒ strict local minimum.

steps.title: Taylor expansion at a critical point
steps.body:
$$f(x^* + d) = f(x^*) + 
abla f(x^*)^T d + 	frac12 d^T 
abla^2 f(x^*) d + o(\lVert dVert^2)$$
With $
abla f(x^*) = 0$ the linear term disappears.

steps.title: Positive definite ⇒ strict minimum
steps.body: If $H = \nabla^2 f(x^*)$ is positive definite, $d^T H d \ge \lambda_{\min} \lVert d \rVert^2$ with $\lambda_{\min} > 0$, so for small $d \ne 0$: $f(x^* + d) - f(x^*) \ge \tfrac12\lambda_{\min}\lVert d\rVert^2 + o(\lVert d\rVert^2) > 0$. Hence $x^*$ is a **strict** local minimum.

steps.title: The other cases
steps.body:
| Hessian at $x^*$ | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| positive definite | strict local min |
| negative definite | strict local max |
| indefinite | saddle point |
| singular (semidefinite) | test inconclusive |

optionAnalysis.reason: Indefinite (eigenvalues of both signs) means $f$ rises in some directions and falls in others: a saddle point, e.g. $x^2 - y^2$ at the origin.
A singular Hessian makes the second-order test inconclusive: $x^4$ (min), $-x^4$ (max) and $x^3$ (neither) all have Hessian $0$ at $0$.
Correct: positive definite ⇒ $d^THd > 0$ for all $d \ne 0$ ⇒ strict local minimum (second-order sufficient condition).
Negative definite gives a strict local **maximum**.

da-2026-2-da-15.shortcut: All Hessian eigenvalues $> 0$ ⇒ bowl ⇒ strict local min.
pitfalls: Thinking positive *semi*definite is sufficient — it is only necessary: $x^2 + y^4$ and $x^2 + y^3$ both have a semidefinite Hessian at the origin, but only the first has a minimum there.
da-2026-2-da-15.verification: $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$: Hessian $2I$ (positive definite) and the origin is a strict minimum ✓; $x^2 - y^2$ (indefinite) has a saddle ✓.

da-2026-2-da-16.approach: Bound the height by finding the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height $h$ can have: $N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1$, a Fibonacci-like recurrence growing as $\varphi^h$. Inverting gives $h \lesssim 1.44\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Sparsest AVL tree of height $h$
steps.body:
To make a height-$h$ AVL tree with as few nodes as possible, give the root one subtree of height $h-1$ and the other of height $h-2$ (the balance condition allows a difference of 1), each itself sparsest:
$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1,\quad N(0) = 1,\ N(1) = 2.$$

steps.title: It grows like Fibonacci
steps.body: Values: $N = 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, \dots$ Indeed $N(h) = F_{h+3} - 1$, so $N(h) \approx \frac{\varphi^{h+3}}{\sqrt5}$ with $\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618$.

steps.title: Invert to bound the height
steps.body:
Any AVL tree with $n$ nodes and height $h$ has $n \ge N(h) \approx \varphi^{h}$ (up to a constant). Hence
$$h \lesssim \log_\varphi n = \frac{\log_2 n}{\log_2 \varphi} = \frac{\log_2 n}{0.694} \approx 1.44\log_2 n.$$
Precisely, $h < 1.4405\log_2(n+2) - 0.3277$: the worst-case height is $\approx 1.44\log_2 n = \Theta(\log n)$.
